title: Butterfly Farms: valuable resource or insect zoo?

paragraphs.text: It's the heat that you notice first — 24 degrees Celsius and 70% humidity. Then there is the lush green vegetation, sporting beautiful pink, yellow and white flowers, whose scents fill the air. As you stand and breathe in the other aromas of the forest, brightly-coloured butterflies flutter past. Some even land briefly on your shoulders or your hair. It is a scene straight from the tropics, which I was lucky enough to witness first hand on the edge of the rainforest in Ghana earlier this year.

But Britons do not have to fly south and risk malaria to see Belizean Blues, South American Owl butterflies or the Philippines Tree Nymph with its white wings and black polka dots. Instead, they can join the thousands who flock each year to the 40 or so butterfly farms, giant heated greenhouses, scattered across the UK. They bring the tropics and their butterflies to our doorsteps, displaying, breeding and often exporting exotic species — but not without sparking intense debate among butterfly lovers.

The farms are insect zoos, which openly admit to being tourist attractions. Though the people who run them are butterfly enthusiasts, their prime aim is to make money. They are also in the frontline of a multi-million pound trade, which sees live pupae (an early stage of butterfly development) — and sometimes adult butterflies — harvested from Third World forests and posted around the world by express delivery. These 'papered specimens' are folded live into envelopes by collectors and then posted, only to be released on arrival a few days later to add glamour to a display for tourists.

There is, moreover, no overall federation for the butterfly farming industry, and no generally agreed code of conduct. Dr Martin Warren, Director of Conservation of the Butterfly Conservation Society, admits that he has no fixed position on butterfly farms. But he says: 'We need to go into this with our eyes open. There are possible benefits to butterflies and conservation — but there are risks as well. Butterfly Conservation would like to encourage best practice and for the farms to maximise their huge educational potential,'

The butterfly farm phenomenon took off in Britain in the mid 1970s in Jersey and rapidly mushroomed. By the 1980s, there were about 100 across the country, with others springing up in Europe and America. The trade has since stabilised — with about 40 farms in Britain, though new ones open and others close each year.

One of the people involved at the start was David Simcox, who helped set up Edinburgh’s Butterfly Farm in 1984 and turned it into one of the city’s top tourist attractions, with about 100,000 visitors a year. He admits that the 1980s boom was partly fuelled by a belief that butterfly farms were a ‘quick way of making money’, though many would-be entrepreneurs paid the price of underestimating the cost of creating the tropics in Britain.

Some species do not cope well with captivity, such as certain swallowtails, which batter themselves against the glass. But many other species thrive in the man-made jungles, and often live longer than in the wild because there are no predators. Inevitably, the fate of the butterflies lies in the hands of their human owners. Successful butterfly houses always have a first-rate horticulturalist. A continual show of flowers is needed, as the butterflies require nectar to feed on, as well as the right larval feed plants for the young. In badly run farms, the conditions are not right for the butterflies to flourish and reproduce. These farms either end up importing so many pupae and butterflies that their business fails financially, or they do not have enough butterflies to show the public. 'It is like conventional farming. If you do it badly, you will not stay in business very long,’ says Mr Simcox.

He believes that well-run butterfly houses are very worthwhile, particularly if they have a sound educational strategy, and this view has some backing from the last man to carry out a detailed study of the British butterfly industry, Dr Mark Collins, the Director of the UN Environment Programme's World Conservation Monitoring Centre in Cambridge. His report, published 13 years ago, led to butterfly farms being brought under the Zoo Licensing Act, subjecting them to the same rules as establishments displaying elephants and rhinos. Dr Collins firmly believes that animal welfare issues also affect insects — and he is particularly opposed to the use of papered specimens of live adults, although he is ‘broadly at ease' with the notion of pupae being transported through the post.

Richard Lamb, the manager of one of the country’s leading butterfly farms at Stratford upon Avon, refuses to take papered specimens from abroad, though he says some British farms do import this way. Very occasionally, if he wants to add to his range of species, he takes pupae from reliable sources in this country. The Stratford farm sends a few hundred live adults through the post each spring to other British farms to boost their stock at the beginning of the season. Mr Lamb says that the adults are picked after falling asleep at 4pm on their roost and arrive at their new home as they wake at 10am the next day. He said: 'They do not even know that they have been moved.'

Dr Collins, who is a registered inspector under the Zoo Licensing Act, says that the British farms are largely well run. ‘In ten years of inspections, not once have I had to recommend the closure of a butterfly farm. I have had to make various recommendations, for example about how the pupae are handled, but nothing more than calling for improvements to a generally acceptable situation. Butterflies are well-suited to small scale enterprises. There are still health, sanitation and disease issues, but that is why the farms need to be subject to the Zoo Licensing Act.'
